papers.title_in_file: Large-scale quantum reservoir computing using a Gaussian Boson Sampler
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section II (setup), MNIST results in Section III, Section IV (Discussion and Outlook); appendices and methods not read
papers.what_it_is: Experiments using a frequency-multiplexed Gaussian boson sampler with more than 400 modes as the reservoir for quantum reservoir computing on classification tasks.

assertions.value: The authors report that giving the output layer access to photon-number correlations between the measured modes (squeezed light) gave the same or higher accuracy than mean photon numbers only, and in several cases an advantage of greater than 20 percentage points.
quotes: resulted in the same or higher accuracy than providing access to the mean photon numbers only, and in several cases resulted in an advantage of greater than 20 percentage points.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one experimental apparatus.
assertions.reader_inference: The advantage is measured against a mean-photon-number readout of the same device, not against a classical machine-learning baseline.

assertions.value: The authors report approximately 60% accuracy on the 10-digit MNIST task, and that the reservoir computer's accuracy was substantially lower than that of a single-layer linear classifier.
assertions.anchor: Section III (MNIST) p.12; Section IV A p.12
quotes: The obtained accuracy on the 10-digit classification task is approximately 60%, consistent with previous QRC results on the same task reported in Ref. [19].
the reservoir computer's accuracy was substantially lower than that of a single-layer linear classifier.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: On this task the quantum reservoir did worse than a plain linear classifier on the raw features.

assertions.value: The authors state that the squeezed-light correlations were not strong enough to rule out generation by a classical light source, and that the system, with its nontrivial optical loss, is likely efficiently simulable classically.
assertions.anchor: Section IV B and F, pp.13-14
quotes: the correlations were not strong enough to rule out the possibility that they could in principle be generated by a classical light source.
it is likely that our experimental system (even when fed with squeezed light), with its nontrivial optical loss, is efficiently simulable classically
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own limit in Sections IV B and IV F.
assertions.reader_inference: The result does not support a claim of quantum advantage.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section 5 (Method), Section 6 (Numerical results), Section 7 (Conclusion), Appendix dataset list; Sections 2 to 4 skimmed
papers.what_it_is: Applies the Nystrom low-rank approximation to KTA-trained quantum embedding kernels to cut the quantum circuit executions needed for the kernel matrix.

assertions.value: The authors state that adapting the Nystrom approximation to quantum embedding kernels reduces the number of quantum circuit executions needed to construct the training and testing kernel matrices, and that the resulting pipeline has end-to-end quantum complexity depending only linearly on training dataset size N.
quotes: effectively reducing the number of quantum circuit executions required to construct the training and testing kernel matrices
we also introduce the first quantum kernel pipeline that has an end-to-end quantum complexity that depends only linearly on the training dataset size N
assertions.certainty_reason: Execution counts are argued in Section 5; the priority claim 'first' is the authors' own.
assertions.reader_inference: The count covers quantum circuit executions only, not classical SVM cost.

assertions.value: The authors report, on four synthetic datasets in noiseless simulation, that the standard approach consistently achieves the highest KTA, and state that one gives up a slight amount of accuracy for a significantly reduced number of quantum circuit executions.
quotes: As observed in the KTA graphs, the standard approach consistently achieves the highest KTA across all four datasets.
if one is willing to potentially sacrifice a slight amount of accuracy for a significantly reduced number of quantum circuit executions
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on small synthetic datasets.

assertions.value: The authors state that all results were obtained using state-vector simulators, on four binary 2D benchmark datasets.
quotes: The methods were implemented using PyTorch and PennyLane and all results obtained using state-vector simulators.
The four binary 2D datasets used in this work for benchmarking the models can be seen on Fig.7.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup in Section 6 and the Appendix.
assertions.reader_inference: No real quantum hardware was used.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Nystrom approximation and the noise compound, whereas the standard approach can tolerate more noise.
quotes: In summary, the approximation and the noise compound, whereas the standard approach can tolerate more noise.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result.

papers.title_in_file: Physics Simulation Via Quantum Graph Neural Network
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Results (Sections IV A to D), Conclusion; circuit-design sections skimmed
papers.what_it_is: Two hybrid quantum graph neural network designs, one speculative and one implementable, compared with a classical GNN on a three-particle simulation task.

assertions.value: The authors report that the models learned simple characteristics in the data with high learning efficiency, but could not determine the more complex behaviors, giving moderate inaccuracy in predictions.
quotes: Overall, the models proved capable of learning simple characteristics in the data, resulting in a high learning efficiency.
However, they were unable to determine the more complex behaviours that were simultaneously occurring, resulting in a moderate inaccuracy in predictions.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one small simulated experiment.

assertions.value: The authors report that on validation data the percent error for the final half of training was approximately 350% for the 1 processor speculative QGNN, approximately 400% for the implementable QGNNs and CGNNs, and approximately 500% for the 2 processor speculative QGNN.
quotes: for the final half of percent error results, the 1 processor Speculative QGNN resides at approximately 350%, both cases of the Implementable QGNNs and CGNNs reside at approximately 400%, and the 2 processor Speculative QGNN resides at approximately 500%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one run configuration.
assertions.reader_inference: The implementable QGNN and the classical GNN perform alike on validation data.

assertions.value: The authors state that the training data came from three particles in a box with the most basic GNN forms, and that the study was completed on a quantum circuit simulator, so real hardware would be needed to determine any real advantage.
assertions.anchor: Section IV D p.17; Section V p.17
quotes: For simplicity, the case of three particles contained within a box was used to generate the training data; likewise, the most basic form of these GNNs were implemented.
Furthermore, this study was completed using a quantum circuit simulator, and thus would have to be implemented on actual quantum hardware to determine any real advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup and limit in Sections IV D and V.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results suggest the implementable QGNN could have an advantage over CGNNs in learning efficiency and accuracy, and that further testing is required to confirm this.
quotes: the results of this study suggest that the Implementable QGNN could have an advantage over CGNNs in learning efficiency and accuracy. However, further testing is required to confirm this.
assertions.certainty_reason: Hedged author suggestion; the paper itself says more testing is needed.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Machine Learning Algorithms for Anomaly Detection: a Review
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v3 (3 Mar 2025); title in file says 'a Review' where the record says survey.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section 2, the fraud-detection passage near the end of the unsupervised section, Section 12 (Concluding remarks); remaining survey sections not read
papers.what_it_is: A review of quantum machine learning algorithms for anomaly detection, grouped by supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning.

assertions.value: The authors state that anomaly detection by quantum machine learning is at its infancy but reveals high potential, and that in several cases there is no knowledge whether strong quantum advantage holds.
quotes: Anomaly detection performed on quantum computers by quantum machine learning algorithms is at its infancy, but reveals high potential.
In several cases, there is no knowledge whether strong quantum advantage does hold or not.
assertions.certainty_reason: Survey-level judgment on the state of the field.

assertions.value: The authors state that, since no qRAM exists, the parallelized encoding of data in qubits is currently not viable because of its exponential data loading cost.
quotes: Given that no qRAM does still exist
is currently not viable because of its exponential data loading cost.
assertions.certainty_reason: Survey-level statement of the state of the field.

assertions.value: The survey reports that a 2022 study with HSBC-affiliated authors demonstrated credit card fraud anomaly detection with quantum kernels on 20 qubits, and that those authors claim a quantum-classical separation of average precision of 15% at 20 qubits.
quotes: In 2022, anomaly detection for credit card fraud detection have been demonstrated by quantum kernels on 20 qubits by authors including HSBC Bank affiliation [160].
The Authors claim that with 20 qubits the quantum-classical separation of average precision is equal to 15%.
assertions.certainty_reason: The survey attributes the result to a cited study and calls it the authors' claim.
assertions.reader_inference: The figure is secondhand; the original study is the primary source.

papers.title_in_file: Exponential advantage in continuous-variable quantum state learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, theorem statements (Theorems 1 to 6), Conclusion; proofs in the supplement not read
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper on learning bosonic continuous-variable quantum states, proving a sample-complexity separation between entangled and entanglement-free measurement schemes.

assertions.value: The paper presents a protocol using entangled measurements and reflected states that learns, up to sign, the characteristic function of CV quantum states with sample complexity independent of the number of modes n.
quotes: We present an experimentally feasible protocol that uses entangled measurements and reflected states to efficiently learn, up to sign, the characteristic function of CV quantum states, with sample complexity independent of the number of modes n.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 1 gives the upper bound.

assertions.value: The authors state that they prove any adaptive scheme without entangled measurements requires exponentially many samples in n for this learning task.
quotes: We prove that any adaptive scheme without entangled measurements requires exponentially many samples in n for this learning task, thereby demonstrating an exponential advantage from entangled measurements.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 2 gives the lower bound.
assertions.reader_inference: This is a sample-complexity separation for state learning, not a machine-learning speedup.

assertions.value: The authors state that analyzing how noise and experimental imperfections affect the separation in practice is left as future work.
quotes: analyzing how noise and experimental imperfections affect the separation in practice, to guide experimental demonstrations of the exponential quantum advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper names this as an open direction in its Conclusion.
assertions.reader_inference: No noise analysis is in the paper.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Neural Networks for a Supply Chain Logistics Application
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Sections VI to VIII (decomposition, hardware results, conclusions); circuit sections II to V skimmed
papers.what_it_is: A reinforcement-learning vehicle routing agent with quantum orthogonal neural network layers, tested on an emulator and on an 11-qubit IonQ device.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the 11-qubit IonQ device QONN performance was quite good for up to 6 qubits, sufficient to capture aspects of the desired behavior for up to 8 qubits, and that at and beyond 9 qubits QONNs were not appropriately captured.
quotes: using the 11-qubit IonQ device
For up to 6 qubits, the performance of IonQ is quite good.
For up to 8 qubits, the performance of IonQ is sufficient to capture aspects of the desired QONN behavior.
At and beyond 9 qubits, we found that QONNs are not appropriately captured by IonQ with its current capabilities.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on one device.
assertions.reader_inference: Usable circuit width on this device was about 8 qubits.

assertions.value: The authors report that a two-truck IonQ execution on 8 nodes with simplified demand satisfied 49% of a total initial rank 2 direct demand of 179.
quotes: Our two-truck IonQ execution on 8 nodes with simplified demand resulted in the following route selection:
The total initial rank 2 direct demand was 179, so we see that the truck successfully satisfy 49% of demand.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one run.
assertions.reader_inference: The 49% figure has no stated classical baseline in the text read.

assertions.value: The authors state that covering the full supply chain with IonQ would be enormously costly, and that the single IonQ run discussed incurred over USD 2000.
quotes: However, the financial cost of this would be enormous.
The run we discuss in this section alone incurred over USD 2000 to run
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this cost limit itself.

papers.title_in_file: Optimal complexity of parameterized quantum circuits
papers.what_it_is: A numerical comparison of parameterized quantum circuits and random universal-gate circuits using expressibility, mean entanglement and a majorization measure.

assertions.value: The authors report that parameterized quantum circuits reach maximum complexity with fewer layers or gates than a random circuit class generated with H, T and CNOT gates, called G3.
quotes: We have found that parameterized quantum circuits, which have a central role for the development of quantum machine learning among other areas, reach maximum complexity with a fewer number of layers/gates than a paradigmatic class of random quantum circuits generated with H, T and CNOT gates, the G3.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical result for the circuit families and sizes studied.

assertions.value: The authors state that circuit topology is crucial, since the less connected circuits perform worse than or similar to G3 ones.
quotes: The topology of the former circuits is crucial since the less connected have a worse or similar performance than the G3 ones.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical result for the topologies studied.

assertions.value: The authors state that the study covers 4 to 8 qubits and 1 to 10 layers, and that a more realistic evaluation considering noise is left for the future.
quotes: We considered from 4 to 8 qubits and from 1 to 10 circuit concatenations with independent parameters
For the future we envisage a more realistic evaluation by considering noise
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope and limit.
assertions.reader_inference: No noisy-circuit results are in the paper.

papers.title_in_file: A Hybrid Quantum Neural Network for Split Learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Section 4 circuit and baseline description, Section 7 (Conclusion and future work); experiment sections 5 and 6 not read in full
papers.what_it_is: Hybrid Quantum Split Learning, where classical clients train with a server holding a small quantum layer, with a noise-based defense against reconstruction attacks.

assertions.value: The authors report mean improvements of over 3% in both accuracy and F1-score for Fashion-MNIST and over 1.5% in both metrics for Speech Commands, compared with the classical models.
quotes: Notably, HQSL achieves mean improvements of over 3% in both accuracy and F1-score for the Fashion-MNIST dataset, and over 1.5% in both metrics for the Speech Commands dataset.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from the paper's experiments.
assertions.reader_inference: The classical comparison model is a simple dense layer, per the baseline description.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum layer uses a low-depth 2-qubit circuit, and that the prototype uses a relatively small and shallow quantum circuit.
quotes: we employ a low-depth 2-qubit quantum circuit within the quantum layer.
Although our current HQSL prototype uses a relatively small and shallow quantum circuit
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that a rigorous theoretical analysis of the noise defense, such as formal differential-privacy guarantees or robustness against adaptive adversaries, remains open.
quotes: a rigorous theoretical analysis, such as formal differential-privacy guarantees or robustness against adaptive adversaries, remains an open area for future research.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit in its Conclusion.
